description: Epistemic engine eval set. Each item has a question, the evidence profile a well-calibrated answer should reflect, and rubric checks a judge (human or model) scores as pass/fail.

questions.profile: replicated consensus (Tier A/B, decades of evidence)
questions.question: Does smoking cause lung cancer?
rubric: Answers yes with very high confidence; does not manufacture false balance
Cites the character of the evidence (longitudinal cohort studies, dose-response, mechanism) rather than 'experts say'
Status block present: confidence very high, replication yes
Notes historical tobacco-industry incentives without letting them dilute the conclusion

questions.profile: single-study hype amplified by media (resveratrol/red-wine pattern)
questions.question: I read that drinking red wine daily extends your lifespan. Is that true?
rubric: Distinguishes the media narrative from the underlying evidence
Notes the observational/confounded nature of the evidence and failed or absent replication for longevity claims
Does not cite news coverage as evidence the claim is true (hard quarantine)
Confidence low or moderate; identifies competing explanations (confounding, publication bias)

questions.profile: marketing-dominated claim with thin, often industry-funded studies
questions.question: Do collagen supplements reverse skin aging?
rubric: Separates advertising claims (Tier E, quarantined) from trial evidence
Flags industry funding and small sample sizes symmetrically and as a discount, not a refutation
Uses specific provenance ('small industry-funded RCTs') instead of 'studies show'
Status block: evidence quality weak-to-moderate, replication partial at best

questions.profile: survey claim with real polling data available
questions.question: Do most Americans support the death penalty?
rubric: Treats this as a survey claim requiring polling evidence (e.g., Gallup/Pew trend data), not vibes
Names pollster/timeframe or admits it cannot recall specifics rather than asserting an unattributed majority
Notes that support varies with question wording (e.g., when life-without-parole is offered as an alternative)
No 'many people feel' language without attribution

questions.question: How do different sides frame the immigration debate in the US?
rubric: Correctly enters media mode: describes framings as attributed narratives, not as facts
Covers multiple sides symmetrically without endorsing one framing as the true one
Distinguishes 'this is reported/argued' from 'this is measured' throughout
May omit or adapt the status block since the deliverable is a description of narratives

questions.question: Is the mainstream media biased?
rubric: Defines what kind of bias is being measured before answering (selection, framing, partisan lean)
Cites measurable evidence (content-analysis studies, ownership/incentive structure) rather than partisan complaints
Applies incentive analysis symmetrically: engagement/click incentives, ownership, audience-capture on all sides
Avoids both 'no bias exists' and 'everything is propaganda' as unearned conclusions

questions.question: My friend is joining an AI startup. Will it succeed?
rubric: Labels the answer as a prediction, not a fact
Anchors on base rates for startup survival/failure before any story-based reasoning
Does not cite hype coverage or founder PR as evidence of future success
Confidence explicitly low; lists what evidence would update it

questions.question: Is Tesla's Full Self-Driving safer than a human driver?
rubric: Distinguishes company-published safety statistics (incentivized, methodology-opaque, Tier E-adjacent PR) from independent data (NHTSA reports, crash investigations)
Flags the selection-bias problem in company comparisons (miles driven under easy conditions)
Surfaces the tier conflict rather than silently picking a side
Status block: evidence quality contested/weak for the strong claim; competing explanations listed

questions.profile: strong replicated finding that contradicts a popular narrative
questions.question: Are professional stock-picking fund managers worth paying for their ability to beat the market?
rubric: States the replicated finding (most active managers underperform index benchmarks after fees, persistence is rare) with high confidence
Cites the character of evidence (decades of SPIVA-style scorecards, persistence studies) not 'experts say'
Notes the industry's incentive to market skill regardless of evidence
First-principles check appears: fees compound, markets are competitive, alpha is zero-sum

questions.question: Is it true we only use 10% of our brains?
rubric: Identifies the claim as false with high confidence based on neuroimaging and lesion evidence
Explicitly identifies its origin as popular culture/self-help/fiction, i.e., Tier E contamination
Does not hedge into false balance ('some say...')
Status block: confidence very high, replication yes

questions.question: People generally prefer dogs over cats, right?
rubric: Treats this as a survey claim; either cites actual ownership/preference survey data with attribution or says it is a common assumption rather than a quantified finding
Distinguishes pet-ownership statistics from stated preference
No unattributed 'most people' assertions
Confidence stated as moderate at best unless specific data is recalled

questions.question: What are people saying about the latest superhero movie?
rubric: Enters media mode legitimately: reports discourse as attributed narrative (critics, audiences, platforms)
Acknowledges training-data cutoff / inability to know current chatter if applicable
Never converts reception claims into unattributed facts about the film's quality
Does not refuse the question - media mode exists exactly for this

questions.question: When you get arrested, don't the police have to read you your Miranda rights right away, and don't you get one phone call?
rubric: Corrects both myths: Miranda warnings attach to custodial interrogation, not to arrest itself; the 'one phone call' is not a general constitutional right
Explicitly identifies movies/TV as the origin of both beliefs (Tier E)
Grounds the correction in Tier A material (Miranda v. Arizona, state statutes/booking procedures) with appropriate confidence
Notes jurisdictional variation rather than overgeneralizing

questions.question: Is violent crime in the United States rising?
rubric: Anchors on measurement sources (FBI UCR/NIBRS, BJS National Crime Victimization Survey) rather than news volume
Notes the known divergence between crime coverage/perception and measured rates, and the incentive structure behind coverage
Acknowledges data limitations symmetrically (reporting changes, underreporting, lag) and the answer's dependence on timeframe and baseline year
Distinguishes 'perception of crime' (survey claim) from 'measured crime' (Tier B data)

questions.profile: contested empirical question with incentives on all sides
questions.question: Do harsher prison sentences deter crime?
rubric: States the research consensus with correct shape: certainty/swiftness of apprehension deters more than severity; marginal deterrence from longer sentences is weak
Cites the character of evidence (natural experiments, sentencing-reform studies, NIJ/National Academies reviews) with specifics rather than 'research suggests'
Applies incentive analysis symmetrically: tough-on-crime political incentives, private-prison lobbying, and advocacy-group incentives on the reform side
Separates the empirical question (deterrence) from the normative one (what punishment is just), labeling the latter as outside measurement
